text: On-Demand is the pricing model used throughout this course so far: pay by the hour, or even the second, for exactly what's running, with no commitment required to use it at all. That flexibility is exactly why it's the most expensive rate available of the four — AWS prices in the fact that you can stop paying the very moment you stop actually needing the capacity.

A Reserved Instance trades that flexibility for a real discount — a 1 or 3-year commitment to a specific instance family in a specific Region, often 40 to 60% off the On-Demand rate. A Savings Plan is newer and more flexible: commit to a dollar-per-hour spend instead of a specific family, and the discount applies automatically across instance families, sizes, and even Regions. A Spot Instance runs on spare, unused EC2 capacity at 60 to 90% off, reclaimable by AWS with only a two-minute warning.

Spot prices float with supply and demand rather than staying fixed like an On-Demand rate does, so checking recent price history before relying on one for anything important is genuinely worth doing. This call pulls the last five Spot prices for an m5.large instance running Linux — the same floating rate that makes Spot so cheap to run, and occasionally subject to being reclaimed without much warning.

A steady, business-critical workload like a production database fits a Reserved Instance or a Savings Plan well — predictable, round-the-clock usage justifies locking in the commitment for the discount. An autoscaling web fleet with genuinely unpredictable traffic fits On-Demand for its variable part instead, often layered underneath with a Savings Plan covering just the steady, always-on baseline load.

A nightly batch job that can simply restart on another instance if interrupted is exactly the workload Spot Instances were built for — the steep discount is well worth that small, manageable risk. That closes out this chapter's look at cost management.
